problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
Summary**

* **a. Verdict:** I have found a complete solution.  
  The minimum number of rectangular tiles required is  

  \[
  \boxed{4048}.
  \]

* **b. Method Sketch:**  
  1. **Permutation of uncovered squares.**  
     The condition “each row and each column has exactly one uncovered unit square’’ forces the uncovered squares to form a permutation matrix: there is a bijection \(p:\{1,\dots ,n\}\to\{1,\dots ,n\}\) such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,p(i))\).  
  2. **Lower bound \(2n-2\).**  
     For each row \(i\) define the left‑hand block \(L_i=\{(i,j):1\le j<p(i)\}\) and the right‑hand block \(R_i=\{(i,j):p(i)<j\le n\}\).  
     - If \(|L_i|>0\), the rightmost square of \(L_i\) is \((i,p(i)-1)\). Any rectangle covering this square cannot extend past column \(p(i)-1\); therefore its **right side** must be exactly the vertical grid line \(x=p(i)-1\).  
     - Since the numbers \(p(i)-1\) run through \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\) exactly once, each non‑zero value \(k\in\{1,\dots ,n-1\}\) forces a distinct rectangle to have right side \(k\). Hence at least \(n-1\) rectangles are needed to cover all left blocks.  
     - An analogous argument for the right blocks \(R_i\) shows that at least another \(n-1\) rectangles are needed (each non‑zero value of \(p(i)+1\) forces a distinct left side).  
     Consequently any admissible tiling uses at least  

     \[
     (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
     \]

     rectangles.  
  3. **Construction attaining the bound.**  
     Choose the permutation \(p(i)=i\) (the main diagonal).  
     For each row \(i\) place a horizontal tile covering \(L_i\) (if non‑empty) and a horizontal tile covering \(R_i\) (if non‑empty).  
     The tiles are disjoint, each tile’s sides lie on grid lines, and every row and column has exactly one uncovered square \((i,i)\).  
     The number of tiles used is  

     \[
     (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2 .
     \]

     For \(n=2025\) this gives \(2\cdot2025-2=4048\) tiles.  
  4. **The case of a single tile (“one = 1”).**  
     With only one rectangle the uncovered squares are the complement of that rectangle.  
     Any row intersecting the rectangle would have either 0 uncovered squares (if the rectangle covers the whole row) or at least 2 uncovered squares (the portions left and right of the rectangle).  
     A row not intersecting the rectangle would have \(n\) uncovered squares.  
     Hence no configuration with a single tile can satisfy “exactly one uncovered square in each row and column’’ for any \(n>1\).  

**Detailed Solution**

Let \(n=2025\).  We work in general for an \(n\times n\) board; the answer for \(n=2025\) follows by substitution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Description of the uncovered squares

Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the set of uncovered squares is a *permutation matrix*.  
Formally, there exists a bijection  

\[
p:\{1,2,\dots ,n\}\longrightarrow\{1,2,\dots ,n\}
\]

such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,p(i))\).  
All other unit squares must be covered by tiles.

For each row \(i\) define the two (possibly empty) intervals of covered squares

\[
L_i=\{(i,j):1\le j<p(i)\},\qquad 
R_i=\{(i,j):p(i)<j\le n\}.
\]

Thus the set of all covered squares is  

\[
\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}L_i\;\cup\;\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}R_i .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A lower bound on the number of tiles

Consider any tiling that satisfies the conditions.  
A tile is an axis‑parallel rectangle whose interior consists only of covered squares.

#### Lemma 1 (right side of a left block).  
If \(|L_i|>0\) then the square \((i,p(i)-1)\) (the rightmost square of \(L_i\)) must be covered by a rectangle whose **right side** is exactly the vertical grid line \(x=p(i)-1\).

*Proof.*  
Suppose a rectangle \(T\) covers \((i,p(i)-1)\).  
If the right side of \(T\) were to the right of the line \(x=p(i)-1\), then \(T\) would also contain the square \((i,p(i))\), which is uncovered – a contradiction.  
Hence the right side of \(T\) coincides with the line \(x=p(i)-1\). ∎

Because the numbers \(p(i)-1\) run through the set \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\) exactly once, the non‑zero values \(\{1,2,\dots ,n-1\}\) each appear as the right side of a rectangle covering the corresponding rightmost square of some \(L_i\).  
Two different values cannot be realised by the same rectangle (its right side is a single vertical line).  
Consequently at least one rectangle is needed for each \(k\in\{1,\dots ,n-1\}\); i.e.

\[
\#\text{rectangles covering }\bigcup_i L_i\;\ge\;n-1. \tag{1}
\]

#### Lemma 2 (left side of a right block).  
If \(|R_i|>0\) then the square \((i,p(i)+1)\) (the leftmost square of \(R_i\)) must be covered by a rectangle whose **left side** is exactly the vertical grid line \(x=p(i)+1\).

*Proof.*  
The argument is symmetric to Lemma 1. ∎

The numbers \(p(i)+1\) also run through \(\{2,3,\dots ,n+1\}\) exactly once; the non‑trivial values \(\{2,\dots ,n\}\) give \(n-1\) distinct left sides that must appear among the rectangles covering the right blocks. Hence

\[
\#\text{rectangles covering }\bigcup_i R_i\;\ge\;n-1. \tag{2}
\]

Adding (1) and (2) yields the universal lower bound

\[
\boxed{\text{any admissible tiling uses at least }2n-2\text{ tiles}.}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  A tiling that meets the bound

Choose the permutation \(p(i)=i\) (the main diagonal).  
For each row \(i\) we have

\[
L_i=\{(i,1),\dots ,(i,i-1)\},\qquad 
R_i=\{(i,i+1),\dots ,(i,n)\}.
\]

Place the following tiles:

* If \(i>1\), place a horizontal \(1\times(i-1)\) tile covering \(L_i\).
* If \(i<n\), place a horizontal \(1\times(n-i)\) tile covering \(R_i\).

All these tiles are disjoint because each occupies a distinct set of squares in its row.  
Every row and column contains exactly one uncovered square, namely \((i,i)\).  
The total number of tiles is  

\[
\underbrace{(n-1)}_{\text{left tiles}}+\underbrace{(n-1)}_{\text{right tiles}}=2n-2 .
\]

Thus the lower bound is attainable, and the minimum number of tiles equals \(2n-2\).

For the original board \(n=2025\),

\[
2\cdot2025-2=4050-2=4048 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The case of a single tile (explicit task)

Assume we try to satisfy the condition with only one tile \(T\).

*If \(T\) covers the whole board*, then there are **no** uncovered squares, contradicting the requirement of one uncovered square per row and column.

*Otherwise* \(T\) is a proper rectangle.  
Consider any row that meets \(T\).  
In that row the part of the row to the left of \(T\) and the part to the right of \(T\) are both uncovered (they lie outside the rectangle).  
Hence that row would contain **at least two** uncovered squares, violating the “exactly one’’ condition.  
Rows that do not intersect \(T\) would contain **\(n\)** uncovered squares, also impossible.

Therefore a configuration with a single tile cannot meet the requirement for any \(n>1\).  
Consequently the smallest possible number of tiles is strictly larger than 1; the optimal number is \(2n-2\) as proved above.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Conclusion.**  
The minimum number of rectangular tiles needed on a \(2025\times2025\) grid so that each row and each column has exactly one uncovered unit square is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

The case of using only one tile is impossible, as shown in Section 4.
